tools.title: The FLIPR 🐬 guide to Election Night
tools.summary_raw: When the polls close, how quickly the votes will be counted, and what FLIPR projects in the most important races of 2026.
tools.content_text: Early this morning — or late last night, depending on your definition — we ran our final FLIPR update of the 2026 election cycle . Nate also published an in-depth Model Talk on the state of the race . I’d encourage you to read the piece in full, but here’s the topline takeaway from FLIPR: Our forecasts show good numbers for Democrats — the last round of polling resolved any doubt about that . They are reasonably clear favorites to flip the Senate, and very likely to flip the House. The Senate is by no means certain, but at the same time, the bottom could fall out for Republicans if Democrats meet or exceed their forecasts on a race-by-race basis. Now that the forecast is frozen and FLIPR 🐬 has returned to the depths of the East River , Election Day itself can feel low-key at Silver Bulletin HQ. This will be the first day in many months where we don’t have to think about updating the model. But our reprieve is a brief one, because tonight starting at 6:00 PM Eastern, we’ll have actual election results to obsess over carefully analyze. So beforehand, we’re bringing you a quick guide on what to watch as the polls close, hour-by-hour, according to FLIPR . We know there are plenty of other election guides out there, but this is the only one with special FLIPR content. For races for Congress, we’ll show you our hour-by-hour projections in every race that FLIPR rates as between “Lean D” and “Lean R” or that has at least a 1 percent chance of being the tipping-point race for chamber control. For gubernatorial races, we don’t calculate a tipping-point percentage, so we’ll also show you “Likely R” and “Likely D” races. Note that these are based entirely on our pre-election forecasts of this morning . We’re not trying to run an Election Night model, but we hope this will be useful for helping to detect which candidates are over- or underperforming. 5:30 PM No poll closings here, but our Election Night livestream will begin! We’ll be breaking down the results in real time with The Argument, GD Politics, Slow Boring, and a bunch of other excellent guests. The stream is open to everyone, but paid subscribers will also get access to our live blog . The blog will include our more detailed analyses — and perhaps some of Nate’s hot takes. We’ll also be answering subscriber questions. Once we launch, you’ll be able to find the video and blog at: https://www.natesilver.net/liveblog Nate and I will be writing on the live blog all night, in addition to popping in and out of the stream. We hope to see you there! 6:00 PM Most, but not all , polling places in Indiana and Kentucky close at 6:00 p.m. Both states are solidly red, and only have one statewide contest FLIPR forecasts — the Kentucky Senate race to replace Mitch McConnell — between them. Republicans are almost certain to win that election. However, there’s one highly competitive House race in this group: Kentucky 6. […]

market.title: The FT and Footballco are growing revenue sources through new offerings, events and more
market.summary_raw: Diversification doesn’t just provide new sources of revenue. As the Financial Times and Footballco show, it helps provide stability in a changing media market
market.content_text: By Chris Sutcliffe The Financial Times is an institution, an incredibly well respected news publisher that has ably made the leap to digital-first publishing. Footballco is a rising digital giant, capturing more than 2 billion monthly video views across its portfolio of sports titles. Despite their differences, these two media businesses face a similar need: revenue diversification. It is the same story across the media landscape. Per WAN-IFRA’s World Press Trends report , alternative revenue sources – from events to licensing – account for over a quarter of publishers’ income. It is at least partly defensive, an attempt to transition away from over-dependence on advertising and circulation revenue. However, as representatives for the Financial Times and Footballco demonstrated at Digital Media Europe in London, revenue diversification can also be proactive, based on recognition of a publication’s core appeal. The FT has spent considerable resources in growing a mixed set of businesses delivering significant results. In 2024, revenues surpassed £540 million with an operating profit exceeding £40 million. Its global paying audience across all titles and events reached more than 3 million, including the 1.9 million paying subscribers to the FT. Aled John is Managing Director, Group Strategy at Financial Times UK. He acknowledged that the Financial Times has a well known international brand on which to build, but said that how the group thinks about its constituent publications has changed: “We celebrate the fact we have an amazing portfolio of businesses. We have four main engines: consumer and enterprise subscriptions – for both FT and our Specialist titles –, advertising, events, and licensing, as well as other b2b services. Our CEO [Jon Slade], on his first day, announced the creation of one major division focused specifically on reader revenue, deploying the power of our sales and marketing capabilities across the entirety of our portfolio of titles.… “We are also undertaking a group-wide review of the FT’s products and services to target resources at the highest-growth sectors and demographics while directing investment into strategic growth markets.” Synergies and core competencies It is leading, John said, to a change in the way in which the FT team thinks about its publications, as part of a whole instead of as separate entities. As an example, it will open the doors to cross-selling and bundling across those brands that did not exist to the same extent beforehand. This new ‘flywheel’ approach enables the core brand to support each of its 17 Specialist publications, with the Financial Times itself as the “base,” and the Specialist titles as an “overlay,” John said. “For us diversification is inherent in who we are,” he added. “The focus is… making sure these things are working very coherently together.
